title: GPU Management: Why Idle GPUs Are the New Grounded Aircraft

Utilization, not intelligence, is the next real constraint in AI.

Aviation learned this the hard way. For most of the industry's history, the number that best predicted whether an airline would survive was how much of the day each aircraft spent on the ground.

The reason is structural. An aircraft's costs accrue by the calendar hour: financing, depreciation, hull insurance, scheduled maintenance, crew contracts. Its revenue accrues only by the flight hour. Every hour spent on the ground shrinks the output side of that equation while the cost side keeps running exactly as before. Utilization also sits downstream of almost everything else an airline does. Turnaround discipline, network design, maintenance planning, crew rostering, and spare parts availability all eventually show up in that one number, because a broken operation underneath it keeps planes on the ground no matter what else goes right.

A bigger fleet still helps. More aircraft means more available capacity, plainly and simply. But two airlines flying comparable fleets on comparable routes can end up with very different economics, and most of that gap traces back to one measurement rather than fleet size.

Enterprise AI is running into the same structure, on a different piece of hardware. A GPU accrues cost by the calendar hour too, through financing, depreciation, power, and cooling, whether or not it's doing anything useful in a given moment. Its output only accrues by the compute hour. More GPUs helps in roughly the way a bigger fleet helps an airline: real capacity, a genuine advantage, and still no guarantee of the result that actually decides who wins. Two companies with comparable GPU budgets increasingly diverge based on how much of that hardware is doing something useful at any given moment, not on how much of it either one owns. That same number, like an airline's utilization rate, sits downstream of nearly every other infrastructure decision a company makes. Intelligence has carried the industry this far. Utilization is where the next real constraint is forming.

The Bottleneck Moved From Models to Compute

The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

Six years apart, both events marked the frontier of what a lab needed just to stay competitive. What changed in between has less to do with AI getting more capable, and everything to do with capability no longer being the binding constraint.

The same pattern shows up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. Cost scales linearly with tokens used, and that single fact separates the economics of a proof of concept from the economics of production almost completely. A PoC processing a few thousand requests a month looks affordable. The same workload at production volume can turn into a cost line that never quite clears. The alternative gaining ground is straightforward enough: enterprises acquiring their own GPUs and running models locally, trading a variable, linearly scaling cost for a fixed capital one.

API cost rises with usage, while owned infrastructure stays close to fixed. Past the breakeven point, the trade reverses.

That shift turns the GPU into infrastructure rather than a line item, sized for growth, sized for demand peaks, and therefore sized above what any given week actually needs. Which means the purchase doesn't close the problem. It opens a new one. The day the cluster comes online, the question stops being can we get accelerators and becomes can we keep them busy, and only the first question had a procurement team assigned to it. Signing for the hardware is the part with a deadline and an owner. Keeping it off the ground is the part that quietly decides whether the deal was worth signing.

These deals describe capacity commitments, not efficiency. How well that capacity gets used is a separate question, owned by different people, measured far less rigorously, and considerably further from being solved.

Why Busy Clusters Still Waste Capacity

A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

The mismatch begins one layer deeper.

In the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

The exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that new capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

Intelligence Moves Into the Infrastructure

Maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

Intelligence doesn't stop at the model boundary. The orchestration layer is making real-time allocation decisions the model itself has no visibility into.

Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

Provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every new request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

The discipline is new enough that its tooling and conventions are still forming, and no single playbook has emerged yet for what a mature GPU Management practice looks like. What has settled, at least, is where the constraint moved.

Specialization Frees Capacity; Orchestration Spends It

Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

Specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

How much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming. Neither lever does the whole job alone.

Specialization without orchestration frees capacity that nobody reclaims. Orchestration without specialization has less capacity worth reclaiming in the first place, because the models are still large and the footprint they leave behind is small. Neither lever does the whole job alone; each one raises the ceiling on what the other lever can achieve. Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

This is why model architecture and GPU management are two ways to address the same problem, approached from two different directions that end up leaning on each other. One shrinks what each workload needs. The other decides, continuously, where the difference goes.

A bigger fleet has always been a real advantage, and nothing here argues otherwise. Among airlines with comparable fleets, sometimes even a smaller one facing a larger rival, the winner was usually whichever one flew what it had more completely, carrying the weight of everything the airline did well underneath it. Enterprise AI is arriving at the same discipline from a different direction. GPUs are already installed, already depreciating, already committed. Specialized models and GPU Management are parallel solutions, or bivalent strategies. Specialization shrinks what each workload needs. Management maximizes the return on infrastructure. Enterprises that master both will set the pace of AI competition for the next decade.

blocks.html_en: The Bottleneck Moved From Models to Compute

sentences.en: The Bottleneck Moved From Models to Compute
sentences.zh: 瓶颈从模型转移到计算

blocks.html_en: The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled. It moved up the chain, landing on a different resource entirely.

sentences.en: The scarcity didn't disappear as AI scaled.
sentences.zh: 随着人工智能规模的扩大，稀缺性并没有消失。

blocks.html_en: The first wave of enterprise AI was won on model quality. Bigger models, trained on more compute, evaluated against tougher benchmarks: parameter count and leaderboard position dominated the conversation, and the race produced models genuinely good enough to run real enterprise workloads. That capability arrives bundled with a dependency, though. Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.

sentences.en: Production AI runs on specialized hardware, and today that hardware is almost entirely GPUs.
sentences.zh: 生产型人工智能在专用硬件上运行，而如今该硬件几乎完全是 GPU。

blocks.html_en: GPUs are expensive, supply constrained, and in demand far beyond what's available, and this holds even at the very top of the market. In 2020, Microsoft built OpenAI a dedicated supercomputer: over 10,000 GPUs and 285,000 CPU cores, reported at the time as one of the five largest systems in the world, assembled to train what became GPT-3. At the time, it looked like an almost unimaginable concentration of hardware, the kind of number that made compute look like a solved problem for whoever could get access to it. Six years later, that number reads more like a starting point than a ceiling. By 2026, even the best capitalized labs on the planet were treating compute access as a live strategic constraint rather than a settled one. Anthropic alone was running simultaneous multi-gigawatt commitments across four separate hardware platforms, Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD, layered within months of one another, while Meta signed a comparable multi-gigawatt deal of its own. Spreading commitments across four vendors at once is what compute scarcity looks like when a buyer has effectively unlimited capital and still can't get enough from any single source.

blocks.html_en: The same pattern shows up downstream of the labs, in a different form. Enterprises consuming these models through an API run into a pricing problem more than a hardware one. blocks.html_en: Why Busy Clusters Still Waste Capacity

sentences.en: Why Busy Clusters Still Waste Capacity
sentences.zh: 为什么繁忙的集群仍然浪费容量

blocks.html_en: A cluster full of busy GPUs can still be wasting most of its potential, and the reason is almost always the same one. GPUs run continuously, day and night, while the demand placed on them does not. Infrastructure has to be sized for the peak, the moment training runs, batch jobs, and real time traffic all land at once, which leaves a meaningful share of capacity provisioned and unused outside that peak. Better forecasting could solve that on its own if every GPU could absorb every kind of work equally well. Few can, and that turns out to be the harder half of the problem.

blocks.html_en: The mismatch begins one layer deeper.

sentences.zh: 这种不匹配从更深一层开始。

blocks.html_en: In the first generation of enterprise AI, a GPU's job was largely singular: run inference. Today the same hardware supports training, fine-tuning, quantization, real-time inference, batch inference, embedding generation, and model evaluation, often for the same organization, sometimes for the same model, on the same cluster. Each of these workloads wants something different from the hardware, and the differences run deep. Real-time inference needs low latency above nearly everything else, because a slow response counts as a failed one. Batch work cares about throughput and tolerates delay, sometimes for hours. Training can occupy a GPU continuously for a stretch measured in hours or days. Quantization needs a large amount of capacity, but only briefly. A scheduler tuned for one of these will misallocate the other three almost by default. The failure doesn't always show up on a utilization dashboard either. A cluster can report high average occupancy while several queued jobs wait for a GPU shape that happens to be busy running something else entirely.

blocks.html_en: The exact workload mix varies by organization. The shape of the problem does not. This is also where the aircraft analogy runs into its limit, and the limit teaches something rather than just qualifying the comparison. An idle aircraft can usually be redeployed to any route in the fleet: a 737 sitting in Chicago can fly to Denver instead of Dallas without much penalty. An idle GPU can only absorb a workload whose memory, latency, and duration profile it can actually serve. That difference makes orchestration harder than fleet scheduling, and it's why the question stops being whether GPUs are occupied and turns into which workload should run on which GPU, at what time, with what priority. Buying another rack of GPUs adds capacity and cost, not a fix for the mismatch, and that new capacity can sit in the wrong shape at the wrong moment just as easily as the capacity already installed.

sentences.en: Intelligence Moves Into the Infrastructure

blocks.html_en: Maximizing GPU ROI takes more than a one-time provisioning decision. It calls for continuous, active management of the infrastructure itself, running every hour rather than only at procurement time. What's emerging in response is a distinct discipline, GPU Management, an orchestration layer sitting between workloads, models, and hardware. Its job is to decide, continuously, which workload runs, when it runs, how it runs, and on which specific GPU in the cluster. None of this is exotic in concept. It's closer to what a good operations team already does by instinct, just formalized and running continuously instead of depending on someone noticing a problem.

blocks.html_en: Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game. Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue. Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited. Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.

sentences.en: Intelligence used to sit almost entirely in the model: bigger, better trained, more capable, and that was most of the game.
sentences.zh: 过去，智力几乎完全存在于模型中：更大、训练有素、能力更强，这就是游戏的大部分内容。

sentences.en: Now it also has to sit in the infrastructure, in the layer deciding, moment to moment, which of several competing workloads gets the GPU that just freed up, and at what priority relative to everything else waiting in the queue.
sentences.zh: 现在，它还必须位于基础设施中，在层中时刻决定多个竞争工作负载中的哪一个获得刚刚释放的 GPU，以及相对于队列中等待的其他所有内容的优先级。

sentences.en: Keeping GPUs busy stops being the goal on its own, since busy is easy to fake by running low priority work that could have waited.
sentences.zh: 保持 GPU 忙碌本身不再是目标，因为很容易通过运行本来可以等待的低优先级工作来假装忙碌。

sentences.en: Maximizing the return generated by each installed GPU becomes the actual target, and that turns out to be a far more continuous problem than the provisioning question that came before it.
sentences.zh: 最大化每个安装的 GPU 产生的回报成为实际目标，事实证明这是一个比之前的配置问题更加持续的问题。

blocks.html_en: Provisioning well doesn't make this go away so much as change its shape. A provisioning decision gets made once, at purchase time. An allocation decision gets made constantly: every time a job finishes, every new request that arrives, every shift in priority between a customer facing service and an internal training run. That frequency explains why the decision has moved from something a person handles case by case into something that has to run automatically. No engineer is watching a dashboard at three in the morning to decide whether a finished training run should hand its GPU to a queued batch job or hold it for an incoming burst of customer traffic. Something else has to make that call, continuously, and make it correctly often enough that nobody needs to check.

sentences.en: Specialization Frees Capacity; Orchestration Spends It

blocks.html_en: Specialization and orchestration solve different halves of the same problem.

blocks.html_en: Specialized, smaller models can perform specific tasks at a fraction of the resource cost a large generalist model would need for the same job, without giving up the quality the task requires. That has a direct effect on utilization. Workloads that once required a single, large model, occupying a large share of a cluster's capacity for the full duration of the job, can instead run on smaller, task-specific models occupying a fraction of that footprint. Capacity that used to be entirely spoken for is suddenly free.

blocks.html_en: How much capacity specialization frees varies by workload and model, but the freed capacity still has to go somewhere or it just sits there. A smaller specialized model only converts into GPU ROI if something is actively deciding what happens next with the space it frees up, reallocating it to another workload, another model, another queue waiting behind it. Left unmanaged, freed capacity becomes a different flavor of idle rather than a win, invisible in a different way than an obviously unused GPU, but no more productive.

Neither is optional if the goal is to actually close the gap between installed capacity and useful output, rather than shifting where the waste happens to sit.

返回文章

人工智能的下一个真正限制因素是利用率，而不是智能。 瓶颈从模型转移到计算 为什么繁忙的集群仍然浪费容量 智能进入基础设施 专业化释放容量；编排花费更多时间进一步阅读人工智能的下一个真正的限制是利用率，而不是智能。

航空业经历了惨痛的教训才明白了这一点。 在该行业的大部分历史中，最能预测一家航空公司能否生存的数字是每架飞机每天在地面停留的时间。

原因是结构性的。 飞机的成本按日历时间累积：融资、折旧、船体保险、定期维护、机组人员合同。 其收入仅按飞行小时累积。 在地面上花费的每一个小时都会缩小该等式的输出端，而成本端则保持与以前完全相同的运行状态。 利用率也位于航空公司几乎所有其他业务的下游。 周转纪律、网络设计、维护计划、机组人员排班和备件可用性最终都会显示在这个数字中，因为无论其他方面如何顺利，其下方的故障操作都会使飞机保持在地面上。

更大的机队仍然有帮助。 简单明了，更多的飞机意味着更多的可用运力。 但两家在类似航线上运营类似机队的航空公司最终可能会获得截然不同的经济效益，而这种差距大部分可以追溯到一种衡量标准，而不是机队规模。

企业人工智能在不同的硬件上运行相同的结构。 GPU 也会通过融资、折旧、电力和冷却按日历时间累积成本，无论它在特定时刻是否做任何有用的事情。 其输出仅按计算小时累积。 更多 GPU 的帮助大致就像更大的机队帮助航空公司一样：真正的容量、真正的优势，但仍然不能保证真正决定谁获胜的结果。 两家具有可比 GPU 预算的公司的分歧越来越大，这取决于硬件在任何特定时刻有多少功能在做有用的事情，而不是任一方拥有多少硬件。 同样的数字，就像航空公司的利用率一样，位于公司做出的几乎所有其他基础设施决策的下游。 智能已经将这个行业带到了今天。 利用率是下一个真正约束形成的地方。

瓶颈从模型转移到计算

随着人工智能规模的扩大，稀缺性并没有消失。 它沿着链条向上移动，完全登陆了不同的资源。

企业人工智能的第一波浪潮靠的是模型质量。 更大的模型，在更多的计算上进行训练，根据更严格的基准进行评估：参数计数和排行榜位置主导了对话，并且比赛产生的模型确实足以运行真正的企业工作负载。 不过，该功能与依赖项捆绑在一起。 生产型人工智能在专用硬件上运行，而如今该硬件几乎完全是 GPU。

GPU 价格昂贵，供应有限，而且需求量远远超出可用量，即使在市场的最顶端也是如此。 2020 年，微软打造了 OpenAI 专用超级计算机：超过 10,000 个 GPU 和 285,000 个 CPU 内核，当时据称是世界上五个最大的系统之一，组装起来用于训练后来的 GPT-3。 当时，它看起来像是几乎难以想象的硬件集中度，这种数量使得计算对于任何能够访问它的人来说都像是一个已解决的问题。 六年后，这个数字看起来更像是一个起点，而不是一个上限。 到 2026 年，即使是全球资本最雄厚的实验室也会将计算访问视为一项实时战略约束，而不是一项固定约束。 仅 Anthropic 就在四个独立的硬件平台（亚马逊、谷歌、微软和 AMD）上同时运行了数千兆瓦的承诺，这些平台在几个月内彼此分层，而 Meta 也签署了一份类似的数千兆瓦协议。 当买家实际上拥有无限的资本但仍然无法从任何单一来源获得足够的资金时，计算稀缺性就会同时分散到四个供应商身上。

相隔六年，这两件事都标志着实验室保持竞争力所需的前沿。 这之间的变化与人工智能变得更加强大无关，而与能力不再成为约束因素有关。

同样的模式以不同的形式出现在实验室的下游。 通过 API 使用这些模型的企业遇到的定价问题比硬件问题更严重。 成本与所使用的代币成线性比例，这一事实将概念验证的经济性与生产的经济性几乎完全分开。 每月处理几千个请求的 PoC 看起来很实惠。 生产量相同的工作量可能会变成一条永远无法完全清除的成本线。 另一种获得进展的方法非常简单：企业购买自己的 GPU 并在本地运行模型，用可变的、线性扩展的成本换取固定资本的成本。

API 成本随着使用量的增加而增加，而拥有的基础设施则接近固定。 过了盈亏平衡点，交易就会逆转。

这种转变将 GPU 转变为基础设施，而不是一个行项目，调整大小以适应增长，调整大小以适应需求峰值，因此大小高于任何一周的实际需求。 这意味着购买并不能解决问题。 它打开了一个新的。 当集群上线的那一天，问题不再是我们能否获得加速器，而是我们能否让他们忙碌起来，只有第一个问题分配了采购团队。 硬件签名是有截止日期和所有者的部分。 不让它落地是悄悄决定这笔交易是否值得签署的部分。

这些交易描述的是产能承诺，而不是效率。 这种能力的利用情况如何是一个单独的问题，由不同的人拥有，衡量的方式远不那么严格，而且距离解决还很远。

为什么繁忙的集群仍然浪费容量

充满繁忙 GPU 的集群仍然可能浪费其大部分潜力，而且原因几乎总是相同的。 GPU 日夜连续运行，而对它们的需求则不然。 基础设施的规模必须适应高峰期，训练运行、批处理作业和实时流量同时出现，这会在高峰期之外留下相当大一部分已配置和未使用的容量。 如果每个 GPU 都能同样好地吸收各种工作，更好的预测可以自行解决这个问题。 很少有人能做到，而事实证明这是问题中更难的一半。

这种不匹配从更深一层开始。

在第一代企业人工智能中，GPU 的工作基本上很单一：运行推理。 如今，相同的硬件支持训练、微调、量化、实时推理、批量推理、嵌入生成和模型评估，通常针对同一组织，有时针对同一集群上的同一模型。 这些工作负载中的每一个都需要与硬件不同的东西，并且差异很深。 实时推理对低延迟的需求几乎高于一切，因为响应缓慢就会被视为失败。 批处理工作关心吞吐量并容忍延迟，有时长达数小时。 训练可能会持续占用 GPU 数小时或数天。 量化需要大量的容量，但只是短暂的。 针对其中之一进行调整的调度程序几乎默认会错误分配其他三个。 故障也并不总是显示在利用率仪表板上。 当多个排队作业等待恰好忙于运行其他任务的 GPU 形状时，集群可能会报告较高的平均占用率。

确切的工作负载组合因组织而异。 问题的形状则不然。 这也是飞机类比遇到极限的地方，而极限教导了一些东西，而不仅仅是限定比较。 闲置的飞机通常可以重新部署到机队中的任何航线：停在芝加哥的 737 可以飞往丹佛而不是达拉斯，而不会受到太大影响。 空闲 GPU 只能吸收其内存、延迟和持续时间配置文件实际可以提供服务的工作负载。 这种差异使得编排比队列调度更困难，这就是为什么问题不再是 GPU 是否被占用，而是变成了哪个工作负载应该在哪个 GPU 上运行、在什么时间、以什么优先级运行。 购买另一个 GPU 机架会增加容量和成本，而不是解决不匹配的问题，而且新容量可能会在错误的时刻处于错误的形状，就像已安装的容量一样容易。

智能融入基础设施

最大化 GPU 投资回报率需要的不仅仅是一次性配置决策。 它要求对基础设施本身进行持续、主动的管理，每小时运行一次，而不仅仅是在采购时运行。 随之而来的是一个独特的学科，GPU 管理，一个位于工作负载、模型和硬件之间的编排层。 它的工作是持续决定运行哪个工作负载、何时运行、如何运行以及在集群中的哪个特定 GPU 上运行。 这些在概念上都不是奇特的。 它更接近于一个优秀的运营团队凭本能所做的事情，只是形式化并持续运行，而不是依赖于有人注意到问题。

智能并不仅仅停留在模型边界。 编排层正在做出模型本身无法看到的实时分配决策。

过去，智力几乎完全存在于模型中：更大、训练有素、能力更强，这就是游戏的大部分内容。 现在，它还必须位于基础设施中，在层中时刻决定多个竞争工作负载中的哪一个获得刚刚释放的 GPU，以及相对于队列中等待的其他所有内容的优先级。 保持 GPU 忙碌本身不再是目标，因为很容易通过运行本来可以等待的低优先级工作来假装忙碌。 最大化每个安装的 GPU 产生的回报成为实际目标，事实证明这是一个比之前的配置问题更加持续的问题。

良好的配置并不能消除这种情况，而只能改变其形状。 供应决策在购买时做出一次。 分配决策不断做出：每次工作完成时、每一个新请求到达时、面向客户的服务和内部培训运行之间的优先级每次转变。 这种频率解释了为什么决策已经从一个人逐案处理的事情转变为必须自动运行的事情。 没有工程师会在凌晨三点观看仪表板来决定完成的训练运行是否应该将其 GPU 交给排队的批处理作业，或者保留它以等待即将到来的客户流量爆发。 必须有其他东西不断地进行该调用，并且足够频繁地正确调用，以至于没有人需要检查。

该学科还很新，其工具和惯例仍在形成中，而且尚未出现任何关于成熟 GPU 管理实践的手册。 至少，约束的转移方向已经解决了。

专业化释放能力；编排花费它

专业化和编排解决同一问题的不同部分。

专门的小型模型可以以大型通才模型完成相同工作所需资源成本的一小部分来执行特定任务，而不会放弃任务所需的质量。 这对利用率有直接影响。 曾经需要单个大型模型（在整个作业期间占用集群容量的很大一部分）的工作负载可以在较小的、特定于任务的模型上运行，只占用一小部分空间。 以前完全需要的容量突然变得免费了。

专业化释放的容量因工作负载和模型而异，但释放的容量仍然必须转移到某个地方，或者只是坐在那里。 只有当某些东西主动决定接下来会发生什么以及它释放的空间，将其重新分配给另一个工作负载、另一个模型、另一个在其后面等待的队列时，较小的专用模型才会转换为 GPU ROI。 如果不进行管理，释放的容量会变成一种不同的闲置而不是胜利，其隐形方式与明显未使用的 GPU 不同，但效率并没有提高。

没有编排的专业化释放了无人回收的能力。 没有专门化的编排具有较少的值得回收的容量。 这两个杠杆都无法单独完成全部工作。

没有编排的专业化释放了无人回收的容量。 没有专门化的编排首先具有较少值得回收的容量，因为模型仍然很大并且它们留下的足迹很小。 这两个杠杆都无法单独完成全部工作。每个杠杆都提高了另一个杠杆所能实现的上限。 如果目标是真正缩小装机容量和有用产出之间的差距，而不是转移废物恰好存在的地方，那么这两种方法都不是可选的。

这就是为什么模型架构和 GPU 管理是解决同一问题的两种方法，从两个不同的方向进行处理，最终相互依赖。 缩小每个工作负载的需求。 另一个人不断地决定差异的去向。

更大的舰队一直是一个真正的优势，没有什么可以反驳的。 在拥有可比机队的航空公司中，有时即使规模较小的航空公司面对规模较大的竞争对手，获胜者通常是飞行能力更完整、承担了该航空公司在其之下所做的一切的重量的航空公司。 企业人工智能正在从不同的方向走向同一学科。 GPU 已经安装、已经折旧、已经承诺。 专用模型和 GPU 管理是并行解决方案或二价策略。 专业化缩小了每个工作负载的需求。 管理最大化基础设施的回报。 掌握这两点的企业将决定未来十年人工智能竞争的步伐。
